Summer break often causes the “summer slide,” the loss of academic skills students worked hard to build during the school year. To prevent this, many schools require summer projects. While some argue that students should design their own projects to follow their interests, I believe summer projects should be teacher-designed. Teacher-designed projects ensure academic rigor, equity, and clear learning goals while still allowing for limited student choice.

First, teacher-designed projects align with curriculum standards and target the specific skills students need for the next grade level. Teachers know what knowledge and abilities are essential for success in their upcoming courses. For example, an eighth-grade math teacher can design a summer packet reviewing linear equations and introductory geometry because those skills are prerequisites for Algebra I. A student-designed project, such as a cooking blog that uses fractions, might be engaging but may not cover all the necessary math standards. Similarly, an English teacher can assign a summer reading list that builds background for the fall study of American literature, selecting novels like *To Kill a Mockingbird* or *The Great Gatsby* and pairing them with guided questions. This purposeful alignment helps ensure that summer work reinforces the right knowledge.

Second, teacher-designed projects promote equity and provide clear structure. Not all students have parents or resources to help them design meaningful academic projects. An open-ended “create your own project” assignment can widen achievement gaps: affluent students might produce elaborate science experiments with parental guidance, while other students may struggle to find direction or choose tasks that are not academically challenging. A teacher-designed project gives every student the same clear instructions, rubric, and list of required materials. For instance, a teacher might create a summer journal with daily prompts and require only a notebook and pencil, making the work accessible to all learners. Teachers can also provide templates and checklists that support students who need extra scaffolding. This shared structure is fairer and more likely to keep all students learning.

Some may object that student-designed projects increase engagement because students choose topics they care about. This concern is valid, but teacher-designed projects can include meaningful choice within clear boundaries. For example, a history teacher might ask students to choose any decade of the twentieth century and create an annotated timeline, or a science teacher might allow students to select between a plant-growth experiment and a weather observation log. This approach gives students a sense of ownership while preserving the teacher’s expert learning objectives. Motivation and academic rigor can therefore coexist.

In conclusion, summer projects should be teacher-designed. Teachers possess the curricular knowledge to target essential skills, the ability to create equitable structures for all learners, and the flexibility to include student choice within a well-crafted assignment. By trusting teachers to design summer work, schools can more reliably prevent summer learning loss and prepare students for the year ahead.

While the purpose of summer projects is to prevent learning loss, the way they are designed often determines whether students truly benefit or merely complete busywork. Some schools require these projects, but the crucial question is who should shape them. Although teacher-designed assignments can ensure academic rigor, summer projects should be student-designed because they foster genuine ownership, allow for personalized learning, and develop real-world skills that generic assignments cannot.

When students design their own summer projects, they take ownership of their learning. A teacher-designed packet may feel like an extension of the classroom, something to finish as quickly as possible. In contrast, a project born from a student’s own curiosity creates intrinsic motivation. For example, a student who loves skateboarding might design a summer project to research the physics of skatepark ramps, build a small model, and document the forces involved. Because the topic matters to the student personally, the work becomes a passion project rather than an obligation. This ownership leads to deeper engagement and more meaningful retention than completing worksheets on topics chosen by someone else.

Student-designed projects also allow for personalized learning that meets each child’s interests, strengths, and needs. In any classroom, students have widely different abilities and backgrounds. A teacher-designed project, no matter how well intentioned, cannot fit every learner. One student may struggle with a required five-page research paper on a historical figure, while another may find it too easy. If students design their own projects, however, a reluctant reader might choose to create a graphic novel comparing two summer books, while an advanced science enthusiast might conduct a water-quality study at a local pond. Both are learning, but each is challenged appropriately. This flexibility ensures that summer work reinforces skills without causing frustration or boredom.

Critics may argue that teacher-designed projects maintain academic consistency and hold students accountable to grade-level standards. While consistency has some value, it often comes at the cost of creativity. The solution is not to eliminate teacher involvement entirely; instead, teachers can provide a framework, such as requiring students to include research, a product, and a reflection, while allowing students to choose the topic and format. This guided choice preserves academic expectations while giving students freedom. For instance, a teacher might require every student to keep a summer journal, but one student could document a family garden’s growth, while another interviews older relatives about their childhood summers. The standard is met, but the learning is personal.

Ultimately, summer should be a time when students discover that learning happens everywhere, not just in school. Student-designed projects teach time management, self-direction, and creative problem-solving—skills that standardized assignments rarely address. When students are trusted to design their own summer work, they learn to set goals, manage a long-term task, and take pride in the result. These are the very habits that will serve them in college, careers, and life. Therefore, schools should move away from rigid, teacher-designed summer assignments and instead empower students to design projects that ignite their curiosity and keep their minds active all summer long.

I agree with the principal’s decision to require every student to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. Extracurricular activities teach lessons that cannot always be learned in a classroom. A student who joins a sports team learns discipline, teamwork, and how to handle both victory and defeat. A student who works on the yearbook practices meeting deadlines, collaborating with peers, and paying attention to detail. A student who serves on the student council develops public speaking, negotiation, and leadership skills. These experiences build time management, responsibility, and problem-solving abilities that are essential in college, careers, and adult life. For example, a shy student who joins the drama club may discover confidence through rehearsals and performances, while a student who joins a robotics club may learn how to persist through failure until a design finally works. Requiring participation pushes students beyond their comfort zones and gives them chances to grow.

In addition, being involved in an extracurricular activity helps students feel more connected to their school community. Students who are part of a club, team, or organization often form friendships with peers who share their interests. They also build positive relationships with teachers, coaches, and mentors. This sense of belonging can improve attendance, behavior, and motivation. A student who looks forward to debate practice or art club after school has another reason to stay engaged with school. Furthermore, students who are busy with constructive activities after school have less unstructured time and are surrounded by supportive adults and peers who care about their success.

A mandatory extracurricular policy also promotes fairness. When participation is optional, the students who are most likely to join are often those who are already outgoing, confident, or have families with the resources to pay for private lessons and travel teams. A school requirement, however, can level the playing field. Schools can offer a wide variety of activities—sports, academic clubs, music, theater, community service, coding, gardening, and more—so that every student can find something meaningful. This is especially important for students who might not have transportation, money, or encouragement to participate elsewhere. The school becomes a place where all students have access to enriching experiences, not just those who can seek them out on their own.

Some critics argue that forcing students to join activities will lead to resentment and half-hearted participation. However, the requirement does not force every student into the same activity; it simply asks them to choose one that interests them. With a broad range of options and the ability to switch after a season or semester, most students can find a good fit. Even students who join reluctantly sometimes discover an unexpected passion or talent. Schools can also be flexible for students with jobs, family responsibilities, or other serious commitments by counting structured activities outside of school.

Ultimately, a school’s mission should be to educate the whole person, not just to deliver academic content. Requiring participation in at least one extracurricular activity helps students build skills, form meaningful connections, and access opportunities equally. With thoughtful implementation and a wide variety of choices, this policy is both practical and beneficial. The principal’s decision deserves support, because it gives every student a better chance to grow inside and outside the classroom.

Critics often say that forced participation breeds resentment and half-hearted effort. That concern is real. But mandatory does not mean forced into a single activity; it means required to choose something. A student who hates basketball can join the environmental club. Someone who freezes on stage can manage lights for the winter musical. This flexibility preserves student agency while still opening doors. For some, the first reluctant step into a club meeting turns into the first place they feel at home.

There is also a practical argument. Employers and colleges constantly ask for more than grades. They want evidence of teamwork, initiative, and commitment. A transcript full of A’s tells only part of the story. Serving on student council, editing the literary magazine, or volunteering as a peer tutor demonstrates that a student can set goals, resolve conflicts, and follow through outside the pressure of tests. By making one activity mandatory, the school ensures that every graduate leaves with at least one concrete example of that growth.

I understand the worry about overbooked students. Some teenagers work to help support their families, care for younger siblings, or manage health challenges. A rigid policy could punish them unfairly. That is why the school should offer low-time-commitment options, such as a monthly book club or a Saturday park cleanup, and should grant exceptions on a case-by-case basis. A thoughtful version of this policy would not ignore real hardships; it would simply set the default expectation that everyone belongs to something beyond their class schedule.

What finally convinces me is a memory from my freshman year. I almost did not try out for the school play because I was afraid of forgetting lines. My friend dragged me to auditions. When our principal announced that every student would be required to join at least one extracurricular activity, I understood the impulse. Sports teams, the yearbook staff, and student council all teach collaboration, time management, and pride. But I disagree with the decision, not because these activities lack value, but because forcing them on every student may do more harm than good.

The first problem is time. Many students already carry demanding schedules that a mandate fails to respect. Consider a junior who takes three Advanced Placement classes, works twenty hours a week at a grocery store to help support her family, and cares for a younger sibling while her parents work evenings. Adding a mandatory club meeting until five o’clock does not make her better rounded; it makes her exhausted. For students like her, an extracurricular is not an enrichment opportunity but a source of stress, late nights, and declining grades. The principal might argue that she could choose a low-commitment activity, but even an hour a week can feel impossible when a student is already stretched thin. A requirement turns what should be a welcome break into another chore.

There is also a danger in treating all extracurriculars as equally accessible. Some activities require fees for uniforms, equipment, or trips. Others depend on reliable transportation after school. Students without cars, bus access, or money may find their choices silently limited. Yes, the school can offer free clubs on campus, but those may not align with a student’s interests or schedule. The result is often a handful of students awkwardly signing up for whatever fits, not discovering a genuine passion. That is compliance, not growth.

Perhaps the strongest argument against the mandate is that it misunderstands motivation. The magic of an extracurricular comes from choosing it willingly. A student who joins a robotics team because he is fascinated by engineering will stay late, solve problems, and learn far more than any graduation requirement could demand. The same student, told he must join something, may pick the easiest option and count the minutes until he can leave. When participation becomes a box to check, the spirit of curiosity and commitment drains away. Schools already have plenty of required classes; preserving some spaces where students opt in keeps those spaces alive and meaningful.

I recognize that some students need a gentle nudge. Many would never discover debate, theater, or cross-country without encouragement. The solution, however, is not a blanket rule. Counselors and teachers can invite students personally, reduce barriers by offering varied clubs during lunch or rotating activity periods, and celebrate participation without punishing those who cannot join. A school can make extracurriculars attractive and accessible without making them compulsory.

If we truly value the skills these activities build, we should trust students to choose them. Let a student fall in love with the yearbook, not be assigned to it. Otherwise, we risk measuring involvement while missing the very growth we hoped to inspire.

The moment an activity becomes compulsory, it loses the voluntary spark that made it valuable in the first

Dear Principal,

I am writing to express my strong support for Policy 1, which allows students to bring cell phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, as long as they are turned off during class. This balanced approach is better for students, families, and the school community than a complete ban.

First, allowing phones at school improves safety and communication. Many students use their phones to arrange rides, check on family schedules, or respond to important messages from parents. In an emergency, a student can quickly contact a parent or guardian, which is especially valuable during after-school activities or unexpected situations. While the school office has phones, a personal phone provides an immediate and direct line of communication that can bring real peace of mind to families.

Second, Policy 1 teaches students how to manage technology responsibly. In college and the workplace, people are expected to use phones appropriately: staying focused during meetings or classes and using devices during breaks. By setting clear rules—phones off during instructional time, allowed during free periods—the school helps students practice self-control and respect for boundaries. A total ban avoids this important lesson and may even make phones more tempting because they are forbidden. When students know they will have a chance to use their phones at lunch, they are more likely to keep them put away during class.

Third, free time is an important part of the school day. Lunch periods and other breaks give students a chance to relax and recharge. Listening to music, playing a quick game, or texting a friend can reduce stress and help students return to class ready to learn. If phones are banned entirely, many students will still bring them to school, but they will hide them and use them secretly. This creates unnecessary conflict between students and staff.

Some people may worry that phones will distract students during class. However, Policy 1 directly addresses this concern by requiring phones to be turned off and put away during instructional time. Teachers can enforce this rule with clear consequences, such as confiscating a phone if it is used in class. This approach is more honest and practical than an outright ban because it acknowledges that phones are part of modern life and gives students a supervised, appropriate time to use them.

In conclusion, Policy 1 is the better choice. It keeps classrooms focused, supports student safety, teaches responsible technology use, and gives students a needed break during free time. I hope you will adopt this fair and practical policy.

Sincerely,  
[Student Name]

Dear Principal,

I am writing about the proposed policy that would require students to maintain at least a B average before participating in sports or other school activities. While I understand the desire to encourage academic excellence, I believe this change would hurt many students and our school community, and I respectfully ask you to reconsider.

For many students with C averages, extracurricular activities are not a distraction from academics but a lifeline. A student who struggles in math may be the first-chair violinist in orchestra or the most dependable player on the soccer team. That sense of competence and belonging can keep a young person engaged in school when grades alone might make them feel like a failure. Remove that anchor, and some students may drift further away from the classroom, not closer to it.

A strict B cutoff also fails to recognize progress. Imagine a student who worked hard to raise a grade from a D to a C. That improvement takes real effort, yet under this policy the student would still be barred from activities. We should celebrate upward movement, not draw a line that tells a hardworking student, “Your best still is not good enough.” A C is a passing grade; it is not failure, and it should not carry the same consequences as failure.

Another concern is fairness. Students do not all begin from the same starting line. Some care for younger siblings after school, work part-time jobs to help their families, or face challenges at home that make studying difficult. A student balancing those responsibilities and still earning Cs is demonstrating considerable resilience. Excluding that student from sports or clubs punishes circumstances that have nothing to do with effort or ability.

Activities teach lessons that report cards cannot measure. Leadership, teamwork, creativity, perseverance, and time management are built on the field, on stage, and in club meetings. If only students with B averages or higher can participate, our school will lose many of its most talented and dedicated members. The band may lose a gifted drummer, the basketball team a natural point guard, the debate club a sharp and fearless speaker.

I understand the concern that some students may prioritize activities over homework. But instead of a blunt B-average rule, we could offer support. Students who are struggling could meet with teachers, attend study sessions, or work with a tutor as a condition of participation. A short probation period could give them a chance to improve while staying involved. These approaches keep activities as motivation without shutting students out.

Please consider that education is not only about the grades we earn but the people we become. Activities help shape that person. I hope you will choose a policy that supports all students, not only those who already excel academically.

When facing an important decision, people often turn to others for guidance. While a single trusted advisor can be valuable, seeking advice from multiple people usually leads to a better choice. Consulting several individuals exposes a decision-maker to different experiences, reduces the influence of one person’s biases, and reveals practical concerns that might otherwise be overlooked. For these reasons, multiple perspectives are a powerful tool for making more thoughtful and well-rounded decisions.

One major advantage of seeking multiple opinions is that it broadens a person’s understanding of the options. Different people notice different things based on their own backgrounds and priorities. For example, a person choosing between two job offers might ask a friend who focuses on salary and benefits, a former coworker who values work-life balance, and a mentor who thinks about long-term career growth. Each advisor highlights a different aspect of the decision, helping the person evaluate the job offers more completely. Instead of focusing only on money or only on convenience, the decision-maker can see the full picture and weigh competing priorities more carefully.

Multiple opinions also help counteract individual bias. Every advisor filters advice through personal preferences and limited experience. A single person may overemphasize one factor or dismiss another simply because it does not matter to them. For instance, when buying a used car, a car enthusiast might focus on engine power and performance, while a parent might emphasize safety ratings, and a mechanic might point out reliability and repair costs. If the buyer consulted only the car enthusiast, they might choose a fast car that is expensive to maintain and less practical for daily family use. By hearing several viewpoints, the buyer can balance these concerns and avoid making a decision based on one narrow set of values.

In addition, multiple opinions often uncover practical details and alternative solutions that no single person would mention. A person starting a small business, for example, could ask an accountant about taxes and cash flow, an experienced entrepreneur about marketing, and a lawyer about permits and liability. Each expert supplies information the others may not know. Even outside formal expertise, friends and family may raise questions about location, customer demand, or time commitment. Comparing these varied suggestions allows the decision-maker to identify common themes, notice contradictions, and ask better follow-up questions before committing.

To be sure, collecting too many opinions can sometimes create confusion, especially if the advice is contradictory or comes from uninformed sources. However, the solution is not to rely on a single person but to seek a small, relevant group of advisors. By deliberately choosing people with different perspectives or specific expertise, a decision-maker can gather useful information without becoming overwhelmed.

Ultimately, multiple opinions help a person move beyond a limited view of a problem. They bring diverse experiences to the table, reduce the danger of one biased perspective, and reveal practical details that improve planning. Rather than simply following the loudest voice, seeking several thoughtful viewpoints helps people make choices that are more informed, balanced, and likely to succeed.

Distance learning can give students valuable opportunities to attend classes from home, and schools should offer it as an option rather than a full replacement for traditional instruction. In-person school provides important social interaction and structure, but online or video-based classes can make education more accessible, flexible, and responsive to individual circumstances. When it is well organized, learning from home can help many students.

One major advantage is that distance learning lets students keep up with their education when attending school in person is hard. Some students have chronic illnesses, disabilities, family responsibilities, or long commutes. Take a student recovering from surgery: under a traditional system, she might miss several weeks of class. With video conferencing, she could listen to lessons, ask questions, and turn in assignments without falling far behind. Students in rural areas face a similar problem, since they may spend hours each day traveling to and from school. Attending online could ease that burden and leave them more time to study, rest, or spend with their families.

Learning from home can also build independence and practical skills. Students in a distance-learning program usually have to organize their own schedules, keep track of deadlines, write emails, and manage digital materials. These habits matter in college and in many modern workplaces. A student who learns to plan a week of assignments and ask for help in an online meeting is practicing responsibility, not just relying on a teacher standing nearby. Some students also concentrate better in a quiet home than in a crowded classroom, where noise, social pressure, and other distractions can get in the way.

Still, distance learning does not work equally well for everyone. Young children, for example, often need close supervision and regular personal encouragement. Other students may not have reliable internet, a quiet place to work, or a computer at home. Schools also matter for reasons beyond lessons: they are where students make friends, practice working with others, join activities, and get support from adults. A student who learns entirely alone may feel isolated and lose motivation. For these reasons, schools should not assume that virtual instruction can replace every part of the school experience.

The best approach is to offer distance learning as a flexible choice and to make sure students get real support while using it. Schools could provide hybrid schedules, online tutoring, loaned technology, and regular chances for virtual or in-person discussion. Teachers should also design lessons that call for participation instead of asking students simply to watch recordings. Small online discussion groups and scheduled conferences, for instance, can help students stay connected to their classmates and instructors.

Overall, students can benefit from attending classes at home, especially when health, location, or personal circumstances make traditional attendance difficult. Distance learning works best when it widens access without cutting students off from the relationships and guidance that schools offer. By making it an option, schools can help more students learn in the way that suits them best.

Summer projects should be mostly student-designed, with teachers providing clear expectations and guidance. Teacher-created assignments can make sure students practice particular skills, but projects that students design themselves are more likely to spark curiosity, build responsibility, and encourage learning that lasts. A teacher-designed assignment might have everyone read the same novel, fill out the same packet, or give the same kind of presentation. Some students will get something out of it, but others will treat it as one more chore to finish as fast as possible. A student who picks his or her own topic, on the other hand, usually has a real reason to dig into it. Someone who loves basketball could collect statistics from professional games and use them to study percentages, averages, and probability. A student who enjoys cooking could research nutrition, test recipes, and write about how ingredients affect health. Both projects build academic skills, but they do it through subjects the students actually care about.

Student-designed projects also teach habits that traditional assignments often miss. To finish an independent project, students have to set goals, manage their time, find reliable information, and figure out what to do when their first plan falls apart. These skills matter in high school, in college, and in almost any career. Imagine a student who decides to plant a small garden. That student might have to research soil, budget for supplies, record how the plants grow, and change the plan when pests or bad weather cause trouble. Along the way, the student learns science and math, but also perseverance and planning.

Choice also makes summer projects fairer and more realistic. Students spend their vacations in very different ways. Some travel or go to camp, while others care for younger siblings, work part-time jobs, or stay close to home. One teacher-designed project may assume that everyone has the same books, technology, money, and free time, and that is rarely true. A flexible, student-designed project can adapt to many situations. A student who helps in a family restaurant could interview relatives about the business and write a report on food costs or customer service. A student without internet access could keep a journal, read library books, or observe wildlife in a nearby park.

None of this means teachers should hand out an open-ended assignment and then disappear. They should offer a menu of possible formats, a rubric that explains what is expected, checkpoints along the way, and examples of strong work. They can also require every project to include research, writing, reflection, or a presentation so that academic standards are still met. Within those limits, though, the topic and the final product should be the student's decision.

Summer projects should be mostly student-designed, because students learn more deeply when they can tie academic skills to their own interests, questions, and communities. Teachers should still set clear expectations, deadlines, and grading criteria, but they shouldn't hand every student the same assignment. A well-planned project that lets students choose can prevent learning loss while also building independence, curiosity, and responsibility.

The first reason is motivation. During the school year, students often do their work simply because it is required. Summer is supposed to be a break from that routine, so a long teacher-designed packet on topics a student doesn't care about can feel more like punishment than learning. A student who loves sports, on the other hand, could study the mathematics behind baseball statistics, and a student who loves animals could volunteer at a shelter and keep a journal about their care. Both would practice research, writing, and analysis, but they would do it through subjects they actually enjoy. When students are interested, they spend more time on their work and produce more thoughtful results.

Student-designed projects also teach life skills. A summer project gives students a chance to practice all of this. Imagine a student curious about local history who decides to interview older residents, visit a museum, and put together a short documentary. To succeed, that student would have to schedule interviews, organize notes, judge the reliability of sources, and meet a final deadline. A uniform worksheet rarely demands that much planning.

Another benefit is that these projects connect learning to the real world. A teacher-designed assignment might ask everyone to read the same novel or solve the same set of equations. Those tasks have value, but they don't always match the varied experiences and needs of students. Consider a student worried about pollution in a nearby park. That student could collect data on litter, research recycling policies, and write a proposal to the town council. The project would involve science, math, persuasive writing, and civic engagement, and it would show that schoolwork can help solve problems that matter.

Some people argue that teacher-designed projects are fairer because every student is held to the same academic level. Fairness, however, doesn't require identical assignments. Teachers can create a shared rubric requiring every project to include research, evidence, reflection, and a final product. They can also approve proposals before summer begins and offer a list of suggested topics for students who struggle to decide. That kind of structure protects academic standards without taking away student choice.

When students own what they study, they become more engaged and creative, and they are more likely to keep learning outside the classroom. Instead of assigning one project to everyone, schools should let students turn their individual interests into meaningful academic experiences.

Others hold part-time jobs to help their families pay bills or to save for college. A student who works several evenings a week may not be able to make it to soccer practice, drama rehearsals, or club meetings. Helping at home or holding a job can teach maturity, time management, and commitment just as well.

Activities are also most valuable when students pick them because they truly care about them. A student who loves writing may pour energy into the school newspaper, while another may be thrilled to join the robotics club. That enthusiasm strengthens the group and helps each student discover new talents. A student who is pushed into a club, on the other hand, may show up only to check off a requirement. He or she might contribute very little, feel resentful, and take a spot that a more interested student would have enjoyed. Participation should come from curiosity and motivation, not from fear of punishment or a missing graduation credit.

Finally, a mandatory policy could increase stress. Students already juggle homework, tests, projects, and plans for the future. For those taking difficult classes or dealing with anxiety, a required after-school commitment could become overwhelming. Club fairs, late buses, waived fees for students who need financial help, and flexible options like occasional service projects or school events would all make involvement easier. These steps open doors without forcing students into commitments they cannot manage.

Dear Principal,

I believe the school should adopt Policy 1, which lets students bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times as long as they are turned off in class. Phones can be useful tools for students and their families, and this policy keeps them from getting in the way of learning. A total ban may look simpler, but it would cause unnecessary problems and would be hard to enforce fairly.

To begin with, phones matter for communication and safety. Many students use them to arrange rides, keep up with jobs and sports practices, and handle family responsibilities. If a practice is canceled, a bus runs late, or a parent has an important message, students should be able to get that information as soon as class ends. Phones also help in emergencies. Students should always follow the school's safety procedures, but having a phone at lunch or after school lets them reach a parent or guardian quickly when they need to. A full ban would make everyday communication much harder for families.

Allowing phones during free time also gives students a fair amount of independence. Lunch and study breaks are when students relax, spend time with friends, and take care of personal business. Some might check homework assignments, look at a school calendar, listen to music with headphones, or text a family member. Others might play a game or scroll through social media for a few minutes. As long as they are not disturbing anyone or breaking other school rules, students should be trusted to make good choices with their own time. School should teach self-control, and a ban takes away nearly every chance to practice it.

The rule that phones must be off during class still protects the learning environment. Teachers need students' attention, and notifications, texting, and social media can quickly pull it away. Policy 1 sets a clear expectation: class time is for learning, and free time can include personal phone use. If a student uses a phone during class, the school can respond with consequences, such as holding the phone until the end of the day or calling a parent. That deals with the students who misuse their phones instead of punishing everyone, including those who follow the rules.

A complete ban could also lead to conflict. Students who rely on their phones for transportation or family contact might hide them in backpacks or pockets. Teachers and administrators would then spend valuable time searching for devices and deciding who broke the rules. Policy 1 is more realistic and easier to enforce because it focuses on when and how phones are used, not on forcing students to leave them at home.

For these reasons, I believe Policy 1 is the better choice. It supports safety, communication, and responsibility while still protecting instruction. By allowing phones during free periods but not during lessons, the school can create a balanced rule that works for students, families, and teachers.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student

When people face an important decision, they often ask more than one person for advice. This is usually a smart move, because different people notice different risks, draw on different experiences, and question assumptions that might otherwise go unchallenged. Too many opinions can feel confusing at times, but advice from several trustworthy sources generally leads to a more informed and balanced choice.

For one thing, multiple opinions give a person access to a wider range of knowledge. No one understands every part of a complicated decision. A high school student choosing a college, for example, might talk with a parent, a teacher, a current college student, and a financial aid counselor. The parent may be most concerned with safety and cost, while the teacher can tell which school would best support the student's academic interests. A current student can describe what daily campus life is really like, and the counselor can explain scholarships, loans, and long-term costs. If the student listened only to a friend who picked a college because of its attractive dormitories, more important issues like affordability or available programs could easily be missed.

Several opinions can also help people notice their own biases. We tend to favor choices that feel familiar, exciting, or easy. Someone shopping for a car, for instance, might be drawn to a stylish model with impressive technology. A mechanic, though, might warn that the car is expensive to repair, and a family member might remind the buyer about fuel efficiency and insurance rates. These extra viewpoints do not necessarily stop the buyer from choosing the car he or she loves, but they make the decision more realistic. Instead of acting on impulse, the buyer can weigh excitement against practical concerns.

Different opinions can also bring out consequences that one person might never have considered. Suppose someone is deciding whether to take a job in another city. A close friend may urge the move because of the higher pay and the chance for adventure. A mentor, however, might ask whether the position offers room for advancement, and a relative might raise concerns about housing costs and living far from family. By listening carefully to all of these responses, the person can consider both short-term benefits and long-term effects. The final answer may still be to move, but it will rest on a fuller understanding of what that choice involves.

Of course, asking many people for advice does not mean handing the decision over to them. Some advice is poorly informed, overly emotional, or shaped by the other person's own preferences. The one seeking help has to judge which opinions are relevant. It makes more sense to ask people who are knowledgeable, honest, and genuinely concerned than to collect as many answers as possible.

In the end, seeking multiple opinions leads to better decisions because it broadens perspective, reduces the pull of bias, and prepares a person for different outcomes. Important choices are rarely simple, and no one sees every side of a situation alone. By listening to several thoughtful voices and then making an independent judgment, people can choose more wisely and with greater confidence.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to urge you to support a national popular vote for president. The Electoral College began as a constitutional compromise, and it has defenders, but it no longer fits the basic democratic principle that every citizen's vote should carry equal weight. The president should be the candidate chosen by the most voters across the country, not the one who happens to assemble the right combination of states.

According to the Office of the Federal Register, each state receives a number of electors equal to its representatives plus its two senators, for a total of 538, and a candidate needs 270 to win. In forty-eight states and Washington, D.C., all of a state's electoral votes go to whoever wins that state's popular vote, no matter how narrow the margin. As a result, millions of votes never affect the outcome. A candidate who carries a large state by one vote earns the same reward as one who carries it by a million.

This system can also produce results that contradict the will of the nation. Bradford Plumer points out that candidates who won the national popular vote still lost the presidency in 2000 and 2016. Outcomes like these make it hard for citizens to believe their votes truly matter. Under a national popular vote, every ballot would count toward a single total, whether it was cast in a fiercely contested state or in one that reliably favors a single party.

The Electoral College also distorts the way campaigns are run. Because most states are considered safely Democratic or Republican, candidates spend their time, advertising money, and promises on a small group of swing states. Voters elsewhere are often ignored, since campaigns assume their states are already decided. Plumer argues that this neglect can depress turnout, because people may feel their vote is pointless when the result seems certain. A popular vote would give candidates a reason to seek supporters everywhere, in cities, suburbs, small towns, and every state.

Defenders of the Electoral College, such as Judge Richard A. Posner, make serious arguments. They say it protects federalism and forces candidates to build broad coalitions instead of piling up huge margins in densely populated areas. They also note that it usually produces a quick, clear winner and confines recounts to individual states. I take these concerns seriously, but I do not think they justify the current system. Rural and small-state voters would still matter under a national popular vote, because their ballots would count toward the same total, and a candidate would still need support from many kinds of communities to win. As for recounts, states already know how to handle close elections, and clear national procedures could be established for a tight presidential race.

The possibility of "faithless electors," which Plumer also raises, is one more reason for reform. Such electors are rare, but no single person should be able to override the choice of a state's voters. The presidency is too important to depend on a process in which electors, rather than citizens, can decide the result.

The Electoral College may have been a sensible compromise when the nation was founded, but our democracy should keep improving. By supporting a national popular vote, you would help ensure that every citizen has an equal voice and that the candidate backed by the most Americans becomes president.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Constituent

Distance learning has evolved from a rare alternative into a familiar part of modern education. While a computer screen cannot completely recreate the energy of a physical classroom, students benefit greatly when schools offer the choice to attend classes from home. Offering this route introduces flexibility, expands accessibility, and allows for a more personalized approach to learning.

Perhaps the biggest advantage of distance learning is the flexibility it provides. Realistically, students lead very different lives outside of school. Some train as competitive athletes and travel frequently, while others care for younger siblings, look after sick relatives, or work part-time jobs to help their families get by. In those situations, a rigid seven-hour school day inside a brick-and-mortar building can force someone to fall behind or even consider dropping out. With video conferencing and online portals, an athlete on the road can still tune into a live discussion, and a working student can catch up on recorded lectures late at night. Instead of forcing teenagers to choose between their personal responsibilities and their diplomas, remote classes help them balance both.

Distance learning also breaks down serious physical and geographical barriers. A student recovering from major surgery, managing a chronic illness, or dealing with mobility issues can stay on track without suffering through an exhausting daily commute. Geography matters just as much. For teenagers in rural districts, the nearest high school might be an hour away, and small local schools often lack the resources to offer electives like advanced physics, specialized coding, or less common foreign languages. Online coursework bridges that gap, giving students access to specialized or college-level classes they simply would not have had otherwise.

Beyond logistics, some people simply absorb material better outside of a traditional classroom. Crowded hallways and noisy rooms can be overwhelming, and students dealing with severe social anxiety or bullying often spend more energy surviving the school day than actually learning. At home, they can create a quiet, low-stress study space. When working with digital materials, they can pause a recording to jot down notes or replay a tricky math problem until it finally clicks. That kind of autonomy does not just improve grades; it also builds the self-discipline and time-management habits needed for college and future jobs, where remote and self-directed work are now ordinary.

Of course, critics point out that remote schooling can feel isolating and cut young people off from everyday social development. Others worry that without direct supervision or steady internet access, students might lose motivation and slip through the cracks. These are fair points, but they highlight the need for thoughtful implementation rather than an outright ban. Schools can combat isolation by requiring interactive video sessions, organizing virtual group work, and still welcoming remote students to join sports teams, theater productions, or on-campus clubs. Districts can also lend out laptops and Wi-Fi hotspots to make sure technology is never a roadblock. Most importantly, distance learning works best as an option, not a mandate. Students who thrive on the social hustle of a campus can always stay right where they are.

Ultimately, giving students the opportunity to learn from home meets diverse needs that a one-size-fits-all classroom cannot always address. It creates breathing room for those with heavy commitments, extends opportunities to isolated learners, and provides a gentler environment for students who struggle in crowds. By offering remote education as a choice, schools are not giving up on traditional teaching; they are simply opening another door for students who need a different way to succeed.

Summer break gives students a rare stretch of unstructured time, and schools are right to want some of that time devoted to learning. However, the question of who actually designs the summer project matters far more than it might seem at first glance. While teacher-assigned work offers uniform standards, student-designed projects are the better approach because they spark genuine curiosity, build practical planning skills, and lead to deeper, more durable learning.

The most compelling argument for letting students take the lead is motivation. During the school year, students work largely under the pressure of grades, schedules, and daily accountability. Once summer starts, those external forces disappear, which is why a stack of assigned worksheets or a mandatory book report often sits untouched until the final week of August. A self-directed project changes the dynamic entirely. A student passionate about baseball might dive into how advanced analytics have reshaped roster building. Another interested in cooking could explore the chemical reactions behind baking and put together a small recipe guide explaining the science. When students genuinely care about what they are investigating, they are far more likely to start on their own, stay engaged over several weeks, and actually enjoy the process. Learning driven by personal curiosity simply sticks better than learning done out of obligation.

Student-designed projects also teach independence in a way conventional assignments cannot. Following a teacher's detailed rubric requires attention, but it rarely demands initiative. When students create their own assignments, they have to define a central question, break a large idea into manageable steps, establish milestones, and assess their own progress. These self-management habits are indispensable in college and the workplace, where instructions are rarely spelled out step by step. Summer is an ideal environment to test these skills because the environment is relatively low-stakes. A student who misjudges their timeline learns an important lesson about pacing without facing a disastrous report card.

Critics often worry that students left to their own devices will pick trivial topics or flounder without clear directions. It is true that teacher-designed projects guarantee every student tackles the same material. Still, this concern can be solved without stripping away student ownership. Schools can simply require a short proposal that teachers review and approve before June. Teachers can provide sample prompts, define baseline expectations for research or writing, and schedule presentations for the start of the school year. Under this framework, the teacher serves as a mentor rather than an author, steering ambitious students toward realistic goals and nudging reluctant ones to challenge themselves.

Finally, student ownership leads to far richer work. Teacher-assigned prompts usually yield twenty nearly identical papers, often completed in a rush. Student-driven assignments, by contrast, generate an exciting range of outcomes: a recorded interview documenting a grandparent’s immigration journey, an illustrated journal monitoring plant growth, or a beginner’s coding project that yields a playable game. Sharing these in September turns the classroom into a community where peers learn from one another’s passions.

Ultimately, summer learning should not just be about preventing the "summer slide"; it should show students that education does not stop when the school doors close. Guided by thoughtful teacher oversight, student-designed projects cultivate curiosity and self-discipline, leaving students with work they are genuinely proud to stand behind.

Whenever we face an important decision, our first instinct is usually to turn to someone we trust. Getting advice from a single person—whether it is a parent, a teacher, or a close friend—can be deeply reassuring. Even so, leaning entirely on one voice comes with risks. To start with, people naturally focus on different aspects of the same situation depending on their background and values. Take a high school senior deciding between an affordable state university and an elite private college that requires taking out hefty loans. A parent’s first priority might be long-term financial security and avoiding debt. Meanwhile, a guidance counselor can speak to graduation rates and career placement, while a recent graduate can give an honest account of campus culture and daily student life. None of these people are wrong; they just hold different pieces of the puzzle. Hearing all three viewpoints gives the student a well-rounded picture of the trade-offs involved.

Consulting more than one source also helps buffer against personal bias. Even well-meaning advisers carry their own agendas. A parent might secretly want their child to stay close to home, or a friend might push for an exciting, risky option just because it sounds fun. In other settings, an adviser might have a financial stake in what you choose. When you only listen to one person, their blind spots easily become yours. But when you gather input from several distinct sources, their biases tend to balance each other out. If three people with completely different interests all point out the same potential red flag, you can be fairly certain it deserves attention. This is why second opinions are standard practice in medicine—no matter how skilled a single doctor is, another physician might catch something overlooked or suggest an alternative approach.

The summer slide, a phenomenon where students lose academic ground during their break, has sparked debate over how to keep minds engaged during the months away from the classroom. Mandating summer projects is a common solution, but the design of these initiatives is crucial to their success. While some argue that teacher-assigned tasks ensure academic rigor and continuity, I firmly believe that summer projects should be student-designed. By giving students autonomy over their summer work, we can foster intrinsic motivation, help them develop essential executive functioning skills, and transform learning into a personal and meaningful pursuit.

One of the primary benefits of student-designed projects is that they elicit genuine engagement and enthusiasm. When students are given the freedom to explore topics that interest them, they are more likely to become fully invested in their learning. In contrast, prescriptive assignments can feel like a chore, often leading to superficial learning and a lack of retention. For instance, a student passionate about environmental science might design a project to create a miniature hydroponic garden or test water quality in local streams. Similarly, a student interested in media could produce a podcast series documenting neighborhood oral histories. These self-directed pursuits not only bridge academic competencies with personal passions but also lead to a deeper comprehension and retention of the material.

Allowing students to conceive and execute their own projects also helps them develop critical executive functioning skills. When a teacher outlines an assignment, they typically handle the organizational labor, including establishing the scope, setting milestones, and defining the final product. In contrast, a student-designed project requires the learner to take ownership of the entire process, from formulating a hypothesis or objective to seeking out resources and troubleshooting obstacles. This autonomy mirrors the demands of higher education and modern careers, where independence and self-motivation are essential. The summer break provides a unique opportunity for students to practice these skills in a low-stakes, flexible environment.

Some may argue that student-designed assignments lack academic substance or invite triviality. However, this concern can be addressed by providing guidance and structural parameters while still giving students the freedom to choose their topic and approach. For example, a school might require projects to address a core interdisciplinary theme, such as community engagement or scientific inquiry, and ask students to submit a proposal and final reflective presentation. Within this framework, students can explore topics that genuinely interest them while still demonstrating their academic skills and knowledge.

By giving students the autonomy to design their own summer projects, we can help them develop a sense of purpose and ownership over their learning. This, in turn, can lead to a more meaningful and lasting educational experience. Rather than simply completing a series of tasks to fulfill a requirement, students can engage in authentic learning that reflects their interests and passions. As they take on the challenge of designing and executing their own projects, they will develop the skills, motivation, and confidence necessary to succeed in academics and beyond. Ultimately, student-designed summer projects have the potential to transform the way we approach education, making it a more personal, engaging, and effective experience for all students.

When faced with important life decisions, individuals often seek guidance from multiple sources. This approach is particularly useful when choosing a career path, navigating complex relationships, or making significant financial commitments. While consulting a single trusted mentor or friend can be a good starting point, relying solely on their advice can be limiting. Gathering multiple opinions is crucial for making informed decisions, as it helps counter personal bias, exposes hidden blind spots, and enables the decision-maker to form a well-rounded conclusion.

One of the primary benefits of seeking multiple opinions is that it acts as a safeguard against individual bias. Each person's perspective is shaped by their unique experiences, fears, and aspirations, which can influence the advice they offer. For example, a young professional considering a career change might consult an older relative who prioritizes job security, only to receive a cautionary warning about the risks of switching careers. In contrast, speaking with an entrepreneurial peer might yield enthusiastic encouragement to take the leap. By considering both viewpoints, the individual can weigh the pros and cons of each option and find a middle ground that balances caution with innovation. This nuanced approach helps to neutralize extreme attitudes and fosters a more realistic understanding of the situation.

Moreover, consulting diverse sources can reveal blind spots and uncover alternatives that might have been overlooked. Complex decisions often involve multiple facets that require distinct forms of knowledge and life experience. In the healthcare sector, for instance, seeking a second or third medical opinion is a common practice. One physician might recommend an aggressive treatment plan, while another might suggest a more conservative approach. By comparing these different evaluations, individuals can gain a more comprehensive understanding of their options and make a more informed decision that aligns with their lifestyle and priorities.

The process of synthesizing diverse advice also empowers the decision-maker by encouraging active engagement with the evidence and promoting critical thinking. When individuals seek counsel from only one person, there is a risk of outsourcing responsibility and passively adopting their mentor's judgment. In contrast, considering multiple viewpoints forces individuals to weigh conflicting arguments, reconcile differing priorities, and clarify their personal values. This intellectual exercise instills greater confidence in the ultimate choice, ensuring that the final outcome reflects deliberate ownership rather than blind deference.

Ultimately, seeking multiple opinions transforms the decision-making process into a rigorous and enriching assessment. By offsetting individual biases, uncovering overlooked factors, and fostering independent critical thinking, a diverse range of perspectives equips individuals to make more informed choices. As a result, the decision-making process becomes more collaborative, nuanced, and effective. By embracing the diversity of opinions and experiences, individuals can navigate complex decisions with greater confidence and clarity, leading to more satisfying and successful outcomes.

Dear Senator,

As I reflect on the current state of our presidential election system, I strongly believe that it is time for our nation to transition away from the Electoral College and towards a direct national popular vote. The Electoral College, established as a compromise by the Founding Fathers, was designed to balance the interests of large and small states. However, this institution has evolved into a system that undermines the fundamental principles of democracy. By adopting a national popular vote, we can ensure that every citizen's vote holds equal weight and that the will of the majority is truly represented.

One of the primary flaws of the Electoral College is the "winner-take-all" allocation rule used by forty-eight states and Washington, D.C. This mechanism can lead to a situation where a candidate wins the national popular vote but loses the presidency, as seen in the 2000 and 2016 elections. According to Bradford Plumer, this outcome not only erodes public confidence in our government but also results in millions of Americans being effectively ignored by presidential campaigns. Since non-competitive states are often taken for granted, campaigns focus primarily on a handful of swing states, depressing voter engagement and turnout nationwide. Furthermore, the possibility of "faithless electors" contradicting their constituents' ballots adds to the instability of the system.

Proponents of the Electoral College argue that it preserves federalism and encourages national unity by preventing candidates from winning solely based on support from densely populated urban areas. Judge Richard A. Posner contends that the system promotes broad national coalitions and produces clear, decisive winners quickly, avoiding the potential chaos of a nationwide popular-vote recount. However, these arguments do not hold up to scrutiny. Rather than promoting national unity, the Electoral College incentivizes candidates to cater to a small group of swing-state demographics, disregarding the concerns of rural and urban voters in other states.

In contrast, a direct popular vote system would provide candidates with a powerful reason to campaign across the country, engaging with voters from all walks of life. Every citizen's ballot would count equally, making it more likely that candidates would address the concerns of all Americans, not just those in key swing states. Additionally, our election systems have routinely managed high-stakes, statewide recounts for gubernatorial and senatorial races without descending into crisis. While there may be logistical challenges in close contests, these do not justify retaining a system that negates the core democratic principle of "one person, one vote."

The Electoral College has outlived its intended purpose and now limits representative democracy in the United States. I urge you to use your voice in the legislature to champion election reform, whether through a federal constitutional amendment or the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. It is time for the presidency to reflect the direct, unmediated voice of the American people. By making this change, we can restore faith in our democratic institutions and ensure that every citizen's vote counts equally in the election of our nation's leader.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Constituent

The widespread use of cell phones has made them a constant presence in daily life. Many people depend on them for communication, directions, and entertainment. But when someone gets behind the wheel, the question of whether drivers should be allowed to use cell phones at all becomes urgent. Although cell phones offer convenience, I believe drivers should not be permitted to use them in any capacity while operating a vehicle. The dangers of distracted driving are simply too serious to ignore.

One of the strongest reasons for a complete ban is the sharp increase in accident risk. Studies have consistently shown that texting, browsing, or even talking on a phone can pull a driver’s attention away from the road. This leads to slower reaction times, less awareness of surrounding traffic, and weaker control of the vehicle. The results can be catastrophic, including crashes, injuries, and deaths. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has identified distracted driving as a leading cause of accidents, with thousands of lives lost or damaged every year. Allowing any phone use behind the wheel puts drivers, passengers, pedestrians, and other motorists in danger.

Some people argue that hands-free devices or voice-activated systems offer a safe compromise. However, this view overlooks the mental distraction involved. Even when a driver’s hands are on the wheel and eyes are on the road, a conversation still demands cognitive attention. Research from the American Automobile Association indicates that drivers using hands-free technology still experience reduced reaction times and a higher crash risk. A phone call, whether handheld or not, can make it harder to notice sudden hazards or respond quickly to changing conditions.

Permitting any cell phone use while driving also risks normalizing distracted behavior more broadly. If drivers feel that glancing at a screen or taking a call is acceptable, they may become more comfortable with other distractions, such as eating, adjusting a playlist, or reaching for items in the car. Over time, this can make distracted driving seem ordinary rather than dangerous, weakening the message that full attention belongs on the road.

In the end, the risks of using a cell phone while driving far outweigh any convenience it might provide. A complete prohibition would encourage drivers to keep their focus where it belongs and help reduce accidents, injuries, and deaths. By treating undistracted driving as the standard, we can create safer roads and protect everyone who uses them.

Cell phones have become a constant presence in daily life, and many people depend on them for communication, directions, and entertainment. But when someone gets behind the wheel, the question of whether these devices should be used at all becomes far more serious. Although some drivers view phone use as a normal, even necessary part of modern driving, the risks are too great to ignore. Drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

The most obvious problem is distraction. A driver who is texting, talking, or scrolling is not fully focused on the road, and this split attention makes accidents much more likely. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, distracted driving claimed 3,166 lives in the United States in 2017. That number alone shows why cell phone use behind the wheel demands stricter limits.

Beyond distraction, phone use also slows a driver’s ability to respond to unexpected events. When someone is looking at a screen or concentrating on a conversation, they may miss changes in traffic, pedestrians entering a crosswalk, or other hazards that require quick action. A delayed reaction can lead to rear-end collisions, pedestrian accidents, and other serious crashes. Even the simple act of holding a phone or typing can reduce a driver’s physical control of the car, especially in moments that require sudden steering or braking.

Some people argue that hands-free devices and voice-activated features make cell phone use safe enough. However, studies show that even hands-free conversations can be distracting because the driver’s mind is still occupied with the discussion rather than the road. In addition, having a phone within reach creates a strong temptation to check messages or notifications, which pulls attention away from driving even when the driver intends to stay focused.

In the end, the possible benefits of using a phone while driving do not justify the dangers. Distraction, slower reaction times, and reduced control over the vehicle can all lead to fatal outcomes. Instead of reaching for a phone, drivers should wait until they arrive or pull over to a safe location. With clear rules and consistent enforcement, we can lower the number of distracted driving crashes and build a safer driving culture. Protecting everyone on the road means recognizing that cell phone use and driving simply do not belong together.

The idea of distance learning has become increasingly common, with many schools now letting students attend classes from home through online platforms or video conferencing. This shift has sparked debate about whether it truly helps students. In my view, students benefit a great deal from being able to learn from home, and schools should embrace this option.

One major benefit is flexibility. Learning from home allows students to shape their own schedules and balance school with other responsibilities, such as part-time jobs, family obligations, or personal interests. For example, a student caring for a younger sibling or working after school can join live classes or watch recordings without worrying about commuting or rearranging work hours. That kind of control over time is especially valuable for students juggling multiple commitments.

Distance learning also offers a more comfortable learning environment. Traditional classrooms can be intimidating, particularly for shy or anxious students, and that discomfort often discourages participation. At home, however, students can engage in discussions from a familiar setting, which may lower stress and boost motivation. A quiet student who rarely speaks up in person might contribute thoughtfully in an online chat or discussion forum, giving them a voice they might not otherwise have.

In addition, online learning can expand access to resources and expertise. Digital platforms often include interactive tools, recorded lessons, and multimedia materials that make lessons more engaging. Students can also connect with teachers and experts from different parts of the world, gaining perspectives that a single classroom cannot provide. For instance, someone studying a foreign language can take online lessons from native speakers, which can sharpen their skills more effectively than relying only on local resources.

Another important advantage is cost savings. Attending class from home reduces the need for daily transportation, and for some students, it eliminates room and board expenses. Online materials such as e-books, videos, and tutorials can also be more affordable than traditional textbooks. For students on tight budgets, these savings can make education more accessible.

Of course, distance learning is not perfect, and it may not suit every student or subject. Still, the benefits are hard to ignore. Greater flexibility, a more comfortable setting, wider access to resources, and lower costs can all improve the educational experience. As technology improves, I believe distance learning will play an even larger role in schools, and I hope more institutions will offer it as a meaningful option for students.

Distance learning allows schools to serve a wider range of students, supports stronger academic outcomes, and prepares young people for a world where remote work and digital communication are common. Every year, schools debate whether summer projects should be planned by teachers or by students. Teacher-designed assignments can certainly provide consistency and academic rigor, but I believe student-designed projects are ultimately more valuable. When students create their own projects, they learn to direct their own work, feel more motivated, and get to explore topics they actually care about.

One major benefit of student-designed projects is that they push students to become self-directed learners. Instead of following a teacher’s step-by-step instructions, students set their own goals, create deadlines, and figure out what resources they need. This kind of ownership builds responsibility and independence, which matter far beyond the classroom. For example, a student interested in environmental science could design a summer project investigating how local pollution affects wildlife. They would have to plan their research, collect and analyze data, and draw conclusions. Doing so deepens both their content knowledge and their ability to manage a long-term task.

Student-designed projects also tend to be more motivating. When students choose topics they are genuinely curious about, they are more likely to stay engaged and put in real effort. That internal motivation often leads to a richer experience than simply completing an assignment someone else designed. A student passionate about music, for instance, might compose and record an album, exploring songwriting, audio engineering, and production. Because the project connects to something they love, the work feels meaningful rather than like a chore.

In addition, designing a summer project gives students chances to practice critical thinking, problem-solving, and communication. They have to make decisions, work through obstacles, and reflect on their progress, which builds resilience. Teachers also get a fuller picture of student learning because they can assess both the final product and the process behind it. For example, a student creating a documentary film must research a topic, write a script, conduct interviews, film, and edit. That single project demonstrates research, writing, technical, and storytelling skills all at once.

Teacher-designed projects may provide structure, but student-designed projects offer a more engaging and effective way to keep learning alive over the summer. Allowing students to design their own work encourages independence, boosts motivation, and lets them explore their interests. If schools want summer assignments to be more than busywork, giving students real ownership is the best place to start.

The principal’s decision requiring every student to join at least one extracurricular activity has stirred a lot of debate among students, teachers, and parents. While some people believe this requirement will help students grow, I disagree. Making extracurricular participation mandatory could do more harm than good, especially for students whose needs and circumstances don’t fit the rule.

To begin with, forcing everyone into an activity ignores the fact that students have different interests and strengths. A musician who would rather spend time practicing piano might end up pushed into a sport they have no interest in. Instead of building confidence or leadership, the experience can become a chore. Students may simply go through the motions without real enthusiasm, which defeats the purpose of extracurricular involvement. When students are placed in activities that don’t match their goals, they lose the chance to explore what truly matters to them.

Mandatory activities can also take time away from schoolwork and other responsibilities. Many students already struggle to balance homework, studying, family duties, and even part-time jobs. Adding a required meeting, practice, or club session can make an already busy schedule overwhelming. A student who needs extra help in math, for example, may have less time to meet with a teacher because they must attend a mandatory activity instead. Rather than helping students become more engaged, the requirement can stretch them too thin and hurt their academic performance.

There is also the issue of stress. When participation is required, students may feel pressure to perform well even in activities where they lack experience or confidence. Someone who is not athletic but must join a sports team could feel embarrassed or inadequate. Instead of enjoying a low-pressure hobby, they may worry about letting teammates down or being judged. For students already dealing with anxiety or self-doubt, this added pressure can be damaging and may affect their mental health over time.

I understand that the principal wants students to be more involved and well-rounded. However, requiring everyone to participate in an extracurricular activity overlooks the fact that students are individuals with different interests, schedules, and comfort levels. A better approach would be to encourage students to find activities they genuinely enjoy and to make it easier for them to join when they are ready. Giving students the freedom to choose, rather than forcing them, creates a more positive environment where they can develop real motivation, confidence, and a sense of belonging.
